situation: Djaouro's uncle is a farmer near Garoua. He says that his rich soil, where he grows maize and cotton, came from the slow breakdown of rocks over thousands of years.
But last rainy season, after a heavy storm, part of a cracked rocky hill fell and blocked a road. Djaouro wonders how the same process can be both good and bad.
sitQA: What is the problem raised in the situation above?
The problem is that Djaouro does not understand how weathering can be both useful and dangerous.
Which good result of weathering is mentioned?
The formation of the rich soil of the farm is mentioned.
What can people do to reduce rockfalls near roads?
They can plant trees on slopes, build retaining walls and drains, and remove loose rocks.

qa.title: Question 1
qa.q: Look at the soil profile. How does weathering form soil?
qa.a: Weathering breaks the bedrock into small pieces (regolith). These mix with humus from dead plants and animals to form soil.

qa.q: How does weathering form mineral deposits, like the bauxite of Minim-Martap?
qa.a: In hot, wet climates, chemical weathering removes many minerals and leaves aluminium, which forms bauxite. It also forms iron ore and clay.
Weathering shapes landforms that attract tourists, gives sand and clay for building, and releases nutrients for plants.

sum.title: I. Positive Impacts of Weathering
items: A. Formation of Soil
Weathered rock mixes with humus to form soil, the basis of agriculture.
soil_profile.png
B. Mineral Deposits and Materials
– Chemical weathering forms bauxite (Minim-Martap, Adamawa) and iron ore.
– It gives clay for bricks and pottery, and sand for building.
C. Landforms and Tourism
Weathering shapes rounded rocks, domes and hills that attract tourists.

qa.q: Why do rockfalls and landslides often happen after heavy rain?
qa.a: Weathering weakens rocks and soils. Heavy rain makes them heavy and slippery, so they slide or fall down the slope.
Heat cracks walls and concrete, water and salts attack cement, and the iron bars inside concrete rust and weaken the building.

qa.q: What is leaching, and why is it a problem?
qa.a: Leaching is the washing of plant nutrients down into the soil by rainwater. It makes soils poor, as in very wet regions.

sum.title: II. Negative Impacts of Weathering
items: A. Mass Movement
Weathered rocks and soils on slopes can fall or slide after heavy rain: rockfalls, landslides and mudflows (as in Bafoussam in 2019).
B. Damage to Buildings and Roads
Heat, water and salts crack walls and roads; the iron in concrete rusts and weakens bridges and buildings.
C. Loss of Soil Fertility
Leaching washes nutrients out of the soil and can form hard laterite crusts, which are poor for farming.

qa.q: Suggest three measures to reduce the negative impacts of weathering.
qa.a: Plant trees on slopes, build drains and retaining walls, and protect buildings with plaster, paint and good maintenance.

sum.title: III. Measures to Reduce the Negative Impacts
sum.intro: We can reduce the negative impacts of weathering:
items: The Measures
– Plant trees and grass on slopes; avoid building on unstable slopes.
– Build drains and retaining walls near roads.
– Protect buildings: plaster, paint and repair cracks; use good cement.
– Add manure and compost to soils to replace lost nutrients.

evaluation: What is the most important positive impact of weathering?
The formation of soil, which is the basis of agriculture.
It weakens rocks and soils on slopes, which can then slide after heavy rain.
Leaching is the washing of nutrients down into the soil by rainwater, which makes the soil poor.
remediation: Weathered rock mixed with humus forms ______.
Broken rock material above the bedrock is called ______.
Weathering in hot, wet areas forms ______, the ore of aluminium.
Rockfalls and landslides are types of mass ______.
The washing of nutrients from soil is ______.
end.remediationAnswers: 1. soil 2. regolith 3. bauxite 4. movement 5. leaching 6. landslides
